title: Holding powers: s5(4), s5(2) and s4
blurb: Know when a mental health nurse can use s5(4), how it links to s5(2), and when s4 is used.
question: At 02:00, Leah, an informal in-patient on an acute mental health ward, packs her bag and says she is going to the railway bridge. The duty doctor is 40 minutes away on another site. You are her registered mental health nurse. What can you lawfully do?

teach.h: Emergency powers to hold, not to treat
teach.body: Holding powers stop an informal in-patient leaving while an assessment for detention is arranged. Section 5(4) is the nurse's power: up to 6 hours. Section 5(2) is the doctor's or approved clinician's power: up to 72 hours. Section 4 is different: an emergency admission from the community on one medical recommendation, for up to 72 hours. In plain English: they buy time safely, they do not decide the outcome.

head: Power
Who
Maximum
For whom
rows: Doctor or AC in charge (or one nominee)
Person in the community, urgent necessity
teach.caption: None of these can be renewed. s5(2) cannot be used in A&E or for out-patients (COP15 18.8).

children.label: Not s5(4)
children.sub: Use the existing section or other routes

items: You are a nurse of the prescribed class: registered in the mental health or learning disabilities field.
The patient is an in-patient already receiving treatment for mental disorder, and is still on hospital premises.
The mental disorder is such that it is necessary for their health or safety or to protect others to restrain them from leaving immediately.
It is not practicable to secure the immediate attendance of a doctor or AC who can use s5(2).
You record it in writing; the record goes to the hospital managers as soon as possible.

items.label: Nurse signs s5(4) record: holding starts
Doctor arrives: s5(4) lapses on arrival

teach.caption: s5(5): when s5(2) follows s5(4), the 72 hours run from the nurse's record (COP15 18.35).
Neither power can be used for a patient already detained or on a CTO (s5(6)).

teach.body: Using s5(4) is the nurse's own professional decision; nobody, including a doctor or manager, can instruct a nurse to use it (COP15 18.27). Before using it, weigh the likely arrival time of the doctor against the patient's intention to leave, and the harm that might follow if they go. Record your reasons in the notes and hand over anyone still held at shift change (18.29, 18.33).

Leah is informal, receiving treatment for depression, and is still on the ward. Her stated plan creates an immediate risk to her safety, and the doctor cannot attend straight away. You try to persuade her to wait, then, judging it necessary, you complete the s5(4) record. Leah may be held for up to 6 hours or until the doctor arrives. You send the record to the managers, explain to Leah what is happening and her rights, and record your reasons.

teach.text: s5(4) is the NURSE's power: 6 hours. s5(2) is the DOCTOR's power: 72 hours. An adult or children's nurse is not of the prescribed class. And if no doctor arrives within 6 hours, the patient is free to leave unless willing to stay; this is a serious failing to report (COP15 18.36).

items: s5(4): MH or LD nurse, informal MH in-patient, up to 6 hours or until the doctor arrives.
s5(2): doctor or AC in charge (or one nominee), up to 72 hours; not for A&E or out-patients.
s5(2) after s5(4): 72 hours count from the nurse's record.
s4: emergency application with one medical recommendation, 72 hours, from the community.

summary: You can now decide when a mental health nurse may lawfully use s5(4), record it correctly and explain how the 6-hour and 72-hour clocks link. You can also distinguish the doctor's s5(2) power and the s4 emergency admission from the community.

A.q: What is the maximum duration of the nurse's holding power under section 5(4)?
A.why: Section 5(4): up to 6 hours from the record, or until a doctor or AC with s5(2) power arrives, whichever is earlier.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is the doctor's s5(2) power and the s4 limit.
whyNot.2: 24 hours is the place-of-safety limit under s135 and s136.
whyNot.3: 12 hours is the maximum extension of place-of-safety detention.

A.q: Which nurse is of the 'prescribed class' able to use section 5(4)?
options: Any registered nurse on a mental health ward
A registered adult nurse with substantial psychiatric experience
A registered mental health or learning disabilities nurse
The nurse in charge, whatever their field
A.why: The prescribed class is nurses registered in the mental health or learning disabilities field (SI 2008/1207, COP15 ch18).

whyNot.0: Working on a mental health ward does not make an adult or children's nurse part of the prescribed class.
whyNot.1: Experience does not change the field of registration that the order prescribes.
whyNot.3: Being in charge does not confer the power; the field of registration does.

A.q: How many medical recommendations are needed for an emergency application under section 4?
A.why: Section 4(3): an emergency application is sufficient in the first instance with one medical recommendation.

whyNot.1: Two are needed for s2 or s3; a second recommendation converts s4 into s2.
whyNot.2: Section 4 still needs one medical recommendation.
whyNot.3: No Part 2 application needs three recommendations.

B.q: A doctor tells you to use section 5(4) on a patient who wants to go home, saying 'I'll see her in the morning'. What is the correct position?
options: You must comply as the doctor has instructed
The decision is yours and cannot be instructed
The nurse in charge must countersign the record
A manager must authorise use of the power
B.why: COP15 18.27: invoking s5(4) is the personal decision of the nurse, who cannot be instructed by anyone else. The doctor should also attend as soon as possible.

whyNot.0: A doctor cannot direct a nurse to use s5(4).
whyNot.2: There is no countersignature requirement in the Act or the Code.
whyNot.3: Managers receive the record afterwards; they do not authorise it.

B.q: A nurse records section 5(4) at 14:00. The doctor arrives at 15:30 and makes a section 5(2) report at 15:45. When does the s5(2) holding period end?
B.why: Section 5(5): where a s5(4) record has been made, the 72-hour s5(2) period begins at the time of the nurse's record.

whyNot.1: The 72 hours do not restart from the doctor's report when s5(4) came first.
whyNot.2: The doctor's arrival ends s5(4) but does not start the 72 hours.
whyNot.3: 20:00 would be the 6-hour s5(4) limit, which lapsed when the doctor arrived.

B.q: Mr Dale, an informal patient, is in A&E awaiting a bed and tries to leave. Can the duty psychiatrist use section 5(2)?
options: Yes, as he is on hospital premises
Yes, once he has been triaged
No, as he is not an in-patient
No, as he has not been seen by an AMHP
B.why: COP15 18.8: s5(2) cannot be used for an out-patient attending A&E; it applies to hospital in-patients.

whyNot.0: Being on the premises is not enough; he must be an in-patient.
whyNot.1: Triage does not make a person an in-patient.
whyNot.3: Section 5(2) is a doctor's report; it does not need an AMHP.

C.q: Mrs Obi, informal on a medical ward after an overdose, becomes distressed and tries to leave saying she will try again. The registered adult nurse in charge calls the liaison psychiatrist, who is 15 minutes away. What is the most appropriate legal route?
options: The doctor in charge or nominee uses s5(2)
The ward manager makes a section 4 application
C.why: Section 5(2) can be used by the doctor in charge of her treatment (or their one nominee) for any informal in-patient, including on a general ward (COP15 18.7). An adult nurse is not of the prescribed class and Mrs Obi is not receiving treatment for mental disorder as an in-patient, so s5(4) does not fit.

whyNot.0: Adult nurses are not of the prescribed class for s5(4).
whyNot.2: Section 136 is a police power; security staff cannot use it.
whyNot.3: Section 4 needs an application by an AMHP or the nearest relative, not the ward.

C.q: You used section 5(4) at 09:00. By 15:00 no doctor or AC has attended. Leah now says she still wants to leave. What is the position?
options: You may make a second s5(4) record
She is held until the doctor arrives
She may leave as the power has ended
The nurse in charge may extend it by 6 hours
C.why: COP15 18.36: if no doctor or AC has attended within 6 hours, the patient is no longer detained and may leave if not willing to stay. This is a serious failing to report.

whyNot.1: The power ends at 6 hours; there is no authority to keep holding her.
whyNot.3: There is no power to extend s5(4).

C.q: An AMHP assesses Mr Lee at home. He is acutely psychotic and dangerous, and only one doctor can attend; waiting for a second would cause undesirable delay. Which route fits?
C.why: Section 4 allows an emergency application in urgent necessity on one medical recommendation, where complying with s2 would cause undesirable delay; it lasts 72 hours unless a second recommendation converts it to s2.

whyNot.1: Section 136 does not apply in a person's home.

reteach.title: Six or seventy-two
reteach.question: Picture the night shift: who can hold, for how long, and what happens next?

blocks.body: The mental health nurse can hold an informal mental health in-patient for up to 6 hours while the doctor comes. When the doctor arrives the nurse's power stops. If the doctor uses s5(2), the 72 hours started when the nurse signed the record. In the community there is no nurse power; in a crisis an AMHP can use s4 with one doctor.

blocks.text: Section 5(4) needs a patient who is receiving treatment for mental disorder as an in-patient. Section 5(2) can be used for any informal in-patient, including on a medical ward.

explain.body: A nurse of the prescribed class may hold an in-patient receiving treatment for mental disorder for up to 6 hours when immediate restraint from leaving is necessary and a doctor cannot attend immediately.

test.q: When does the s5(4) holding period begin?
options: When the patient tries to leave
When the record is made in writing
When the managers receive the record
test.why: Section 5(4) and COP15 18.26: the patient may be detained from the moment the nurse makes the record.

whyNot.0: The legal power starts with the written record, not the attempt to leave.
whyNot.2: The record goes to managers afterwards; the power starts when it is made.
whyNot.3: Calling the doctor does not start the power.

explain.body: The doctor or AC in charge of an in-patient's treatment, or one nominee, reports that an application ought to be made. The patient may be held for up to 72 hours. Not in A&E or for out-patients.

test.q: How many deputies may the doctor in charge nominate to act under section 5(2) in their absence?
test.why: Section 5(3) allows the doctor or AC in charge to nominate one (but not more than one) person to act for them.

whyNot.0: The Act limits it to one nominee.
whyNot.1: The Act limits it to one nominee.
whyNot.2: A rota of doctors cannot all be nominees; only one person may be nominated.

explain.body: If the doctor arrives within 6 hours, s5(4) lapses on arrival. If the doctor then uses s5(2), the 72 hours run from the nurse's original record (s5(5)).

test.q: What happens to section 5(4) when the doctor arrives on the ward?
options: It lapses on the doctor's arrival
It continues until the full 6 hours have passed
test.why: COP15 18.35: if the doctor or AC arrives before the end of 6 hours, the holding power lapses on their arrival.

whyNot.1: The 6 hours are a maximum, ending earlier if the doctor arrives.
whyNot.2: Conversion to s2 needs an application with two medical recommendations.
whyNot.3: The doctor must make a s5(2) report; s5(4) is not extended.

explain.body: In urgent necessity an AMHP or nearest relative can apply on one medical recommendation, having seen the person in the previous 24 hours. It lasts 72 hours from admission unless a second recommendation turns it into s2.

test.q: Within what period must the applicant have personally seen the patient for a section 4 application?
test.why: Section 4(5) substitutes 'the previous 24 hours' for the usual 14 days in s11(5).

whyNot.0: 14 days is the usual rule for s2 and s3 applications.
whyNot.1: 72 hours is the life of the s4 application.
whyNot.3: 5 days is the maximum gap between two separate medical examinations.
